results.blind_working: In Werner's theory, primary valency is ionisable and equals the oxidation state. It is satisfied by anions. Secondary valency is non-ionisable, equals the coordination number and fixes the geometry.
0.02 mol AgCl from 0.01 mol complex means 2 ionisable Cl- per formula unit. For Co(III) with coordination number 6 this gives [CoCl(NH3)5]Cl2.
Count ions per formula unit: [Co(NH3)3(NO2)3] gives 0, [CoCl(NH3)5]Cl2 gives 3, [Co(NH3)6]Cl3 gives 4, K4[Fe(CN)6] gives 5. Molar conductivity rises in that order.
[CoCl2(NH3)4]Cl has only one counter Cl-, so it gives 1 mol AgCl, not 3. A is false. R is true because only ions outside the coordination sphere are precipitated.
Co(III) has primary valency 3 and coordination number 6, so I is correct. The compound ionises to [CoCl(NH3)5]2+ + 2Cl-, which is 3 ions and a 1:2 electrolyte, so II is incorrect.
K4[Fe(CN)6] has an anionic complex. K is +1, so Fe is +2. An anionic complex takes the Latin stem with -ate, giving ferrate(II): potassium hexacyanidoferrate(II).
Ligands go in alphabetical order, ammine before chlorido. Co = +3 (5×0 − 1 + Co = +2). The complex is a cation, so there is no -ate ending: pentaamminechloridocobalt(III) chloride.
Three oxalate ligands give 3×(−2) = −6. With Fe(III) the complex charge is −3, so three K+ are needed: K3[Fe(C2O4)3].
The name is tetraammineaquachloridocobalt(III) chloride. Ammine comes before aqua alphabetically (m before q), and the prefix tetra is ignored when ordering. A is true, R is true, and R explains A.

Statement I: Ni(CO)4 is neutral, Ni is 0, so it is tetracarbonylnickel(0) with no -ate ending; correct. Statement II: [Co(en)3]3+ is a cation with Co(III), named tris(ethane-1,2-diamine)cobalt(III) sulphate; correct.

Ionisation isomers swap a ligand with the counter-ion, giving different ions in solution. In option 3, SO4^2- and Cl- exchange places. Option 1 is linkage, option 2 is geometrical and option 4 is hydrate isomerism.
[CoBr2(en)2]+ has a trans form, which is achiral. Its cis form exists as a pair of enantiomers. Total stereoisomers = 1 + 2 = 3.
[Cr(ox)3]3- is a tris-chelate with no mirror plane, giving delta and lambda forms, so it is chiral. The other three species each have a mirror plane.

A: NO2 vs ONO is linkage (II). B: water inside vs outside the sphere is hydrate (IV). C: ligands exchanged between cation and anion is coordination (III). D: Cl and Br swap between sphere and counter-ion is ionisation (I).

A is true: MA2B2C2 has 5 geometrical isomers, and the all-cis one is chiral, giving 6 stereoisomers. B is false: tetrahedral complexes show no cis-trans isomerism. C is true: square planar MABCD has 3 isomers. D is true by definition of fac. E is false: the trans isomer has a mirror plane. So A, C, D are correct.
Ni2+ is 3d8. Strong-field CN- pairs the electrons, leaving one 3d orbital empty. This gives dsp2 hybridisation, which is square planar.

Fe2+ is d6. Strong-field CN- pairs all six electrons, so two inner 3d orbitals stay empty. Hybridisation is d2sp3, an inner-orbital complex. [CoF6]3- is sp3d2 (outer orbital). Ni(CO)4 and [CoCl4]2- are sp3, using no d orbitals.
Co3+ is d6. F- is weak field, so the complex is high spin with 4 unpaired electrons. mu = sqrt(4 x 6) = sqrt(24) = 4.90 BM.
Ni(CO)4 is sp3, tetrahedral and diamagnetic, so A is true. Ni is in the 0 oxidation state (3d8 4s2, rearranged to 3d10), not +2, so R is false.

Fe3+ is d5. Low spin with CN- gives d2sp3 hybridisation and 1 unpaired electron, so mu = 1.73 BM and I is correct. NCERT lists among VBT's limitations that it cannot exactly predict tetrahedral versus square planar structures of 4-coordinate complexes, so II is correct.
In an octahedral field the t2g set points between the ligands, so it is stabilised and sits at -0.4Δo. The eg set rises to +0.6Δo.
A weak field gives the high-spin configuration t2g3 eg1. CFSE = 3(-0.4) + 1(0.6) = -0.6Δo, with no extra pairing energy.
A: Δo > P gives low spin t2g4 (II). B: Δo < P gives t2g3 eg1 (I). C: the lower set in a tetrahedral field is e (IV). D: the highest orbital in square planar is dx2-y2 (III).

A is true: Δo rises from 3d to 4d to 5d. B is true: Δt is small, so tetrahedral complexes are high spin. C is false: F- is a weaker-field ligand than H2O. D is false: CFT treats ligands as point charges, so it cannot explain CO being strongest. E is true: higher oxidation state gives larger Δo. Correct set is A, B and E.
Sc3+ has a d0 configuration, so no d-d transition is possible and the complex is colourless. Ti3+ (d1), Ni2+ (d8) and Cu2+ (d9) are all coloured.
[Fe(CN)6]4-: d6 low spin, 0 unpaired. [Fe(CN)6]3-: d5 low spin, 1 unpaired. [CoF6]3-: d6 high spin, 4 unpaired. [MnF6]4-: Mn2+ d5 high spin, 5 unpaired, giving 5.92 BM, the highest.
E = hc/λ = (6.6e-34 × 3e8)/(600e-9) = 3.3e-19 J per ion. Multiplying by NA gives 3.3e-19 × 6e23 = 1.98e5 J/mol = 198 kJ/mol.

A is true: MnO4- is intensely coloured. R is true as the general d-d explanation for most complexes. However, Mn(VII) is d0, so its colour arises from ligand-to-metal charge transfer, not d-d transitions. R therefore does not explain A.

I: Co3+ is d6 and NH3 makes it low spin (t2g6), so it is diamagnetic with 0 BM; I is incorrect. II: en is a stronger-field ligand than H2O, so Δo increases and the complex absorbs shorter wavelengths; II is incorrect.
